claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments in a copper matrix.
A nanoscale transition-metal-silicide coating can be applied to tungsten surfaces during composite processing.
The coating will produce a coherent nanoscale silicide interphase at the W–Cu interface.
The silicide interphase will chemically bridge the W and Cu phases.
The silicide coating will reduce W–Cu interfacial energy.
The silicide coating will retard diffusion-driven phase separation.
The silicide coating will retard interfacial void nucleation.
A silicide interphase can retain structural integrity under high-temperature exposure.
The coating will stabilize the W–Cu interface under irradiation.
Enhanced interfacial stability will maintain a continuous heat-conduction path.
The coated composite will exhibit less phase separation than the untreated composite after high-heat-flux and irradiation exposure.
The coated composite will exhibit fewer interfacial voids than the untreated composite after high-heat-flux and irradiation exposure.
The coated composite will have higher and more stable thermal conductivity than the untreated composite.
Untreated W–Cu composites undergo deleterious phase separation and interfacial void formation under the stated service conditions.
Phase separation and interfacial void formation degrade the thermal performance of untreated W–Cu composites.
The intervention is applicable to fabrication of joints between tungsten plasma-facing materials and copper cooling components.
The intervention is effective under combined high thermal loads and irradiation.
The optimum coating composition and thickness are not yet established.
The coating's long-term stability under combined high heat flux and irradiation is uncertain.
Potential effects of the coating on mechanical integrity are uncertain.
